pos: adj. (having sworn falsely; guilty of violating a sworn oath)
etymology: Latin perjurare, from per-, thoroughly, and jurare, to swear — to swear falsely, breaking an oath through and through.
biblical_def:
For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine.

Paul's list of those for whom the law is made sits inside a larger argument that the law is good when used lawfully — not to justify the righteous, who have no need of its condemning function, but to restrain and expose exactly this catalogue of offenders. Perjured persons appear beside liars but are named separately, because perjury adds to ordinary falsehood the specific sin of invoking God's name, or an oath before him, to certify a lie. It is falsehood wearing the garment of solemn truth-telling, and Paul places it deliberately among sins contrary to sound doctrine, treating false witness under oath as an assault on the very idea of a trustworthy word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PERJURE: having sworn falsely; forsworn; guilty of violating a solemn oath by false testimony.
webster_full: PERJURE, v.t. To swear falsely; to forswear; to violate an oath by a false declaration.
PERJURED, pp. Guilty of perjury; forsworn.
Distinguished from ordinary lying by the breach of a sworn oath.
Listed by Paul in 1 Timothy among those for whom the law is made.
Treated as an offense against sound doctrine, not merely civil order.
scriptures: For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;
corruption_summary: A culture in which oaths are rarely sworn and routinely broken without consequence has little category left for perjured as a distinct, graver sin than ordinary dishonesty.
corruption_paragraphs: When almost nothing is sworn solemnly, almost nothing can be perjured in the full biblical sense, and the word drifts toward a merely legal technicality — a courtroom offense rather than a sin against God's name.

Paul's list restores the weight: perjured persons sit beside liars but are named as their own category, because invoking God, or an oath before him, to certify a falsehood compounds the lie with an abuse of what is sacred. The ninth commandment's prohibition on false witness finds its sharpest form here.
roots_summary: Greek epiorkos, a false swearer, from epi- and horkos, oath — one who swears upon, and thereby violates, a solemn oath.
roots_lines: Perjured names false swearing, not merely false speaking.
Paul distinguishes it from ordinary liars in the same list.
It compounds falsehood with an abuse of a sworn oath before God.
The law is made to restrain exactly this kind of offender.
The ninth commandment's prohibition finds its sharpest form in perjury.
usage: For liars, for perjured persons — two distinct, related offenses.
Contrary to sound doctrine — perjury treated as a doctrinal, not merely civil, matter.
The law is made for exactly this catalogue of offenders.

pos: n. (forced or oppressive demands for payment or tribute)
etymology: Latin exigere, to force out, demand — payment extracted by pressure or authority rather than freely given.
biblical_def:
Thus saith the Lord GOD; Let it suffice you, O princes of Israel: remove violence and spoil, and execute judgment and justice, take away your exactions from my people, saith the Lord GOD.

Ezekiel's vision of a restored temple and land comes paired with sharp ethical demand on the princes who rule it: let it suffice you is a rebuke of appetite, and exactions names the specific mechanism of their sin — using political power to extract more from the people than justice allows. The command to remove violence and spoil alongside exactions treats oppressive taxation as morally equivalent to outright theft, not a lesser administrative excess. A restored worship cannot coexist with rulers who still fund their appetites by squeezing the people God has entrusted to their care.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from EXACT: the act of demanding and enforcing payment with rigor or severity; oppressive or unjust extortion.
webster_full: EXACT, v.t. To demand and enforce payment of, with rigor; to extort.
EXACTION, n. The act of exacting; an oppressive or unjust demand.
Distinguished from ordinary taxation by injustice in measure or manner.
In Ezekiel, named alongside violence and spoil as equivalent sin.
Addressed to princes, making it a sin of rulers specifically.
scriptures: Thus saith the Lord GOD; Let it suffice you, O princes of Israel: remove violence and spoil, and execute judgment and justice, take away your exactions from my people, saith the Lord GOD.
corruption_summary: Political language today often treats oppressive taxation as a mere policy dispute to be debated on efficiency grounds, while Ezekiel 45:9 names exactions as sin, grouped with violence and spoil and demanding repentance, not merely reform.
corruption_paragraphs: When exactions are debated only in terms of economic outcomes, the moral category drops out: Ezekiel does not ask whether the princes' demands were efficient, but whether they were just, and answers unambiguously that they were not.

The corrective is to retain exactions as a biblical category of ruler's sin alongside violence and spoil, applicable wherever those entrusted with authority fund their appetites by squeezing those under their care, rather than treating the matter as morally neutral statecraft.
roots_summary: Hebrew gerushah, a casting out or expulsion, here used idiomatically of forced extraction — rendered exactions to capture the oppressive demand on the people's substance.
roots_lines: Exactions names oppressive, forced demand, not ordinary taxation.
Ezekiel groups it with violence and spoil as equivalent sin.
The rebuke is addressed specifically to princes, not the people.
Let it suffice you rebukes appetite, not merely method.
Restored worship requires rulers who no longer exact from the people.
usage: Take away your exactions from my people — a direct command to ruling princes.
Grouped with violence and spoil, not treated as a lesser offense.
Restored worship and oppressive rule cannot coexist.

pos: adj./v. past part. (put down from a throne or position of authority)
etymology: Latin deponere, to put down — to remove a ruler forcibly from the seat of power.
biblical_def:
But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him.

This is Daniel's summary, delivered to Belshazzar, of what had already happened to Nebuchadnezzar: pride preceded the fall, and the fall was total — throne, glory, even human reason itself stripped away until the king ate grass like an ox. Deposed here is not a political event narrated for its own sake but a theological verdict pronounced on every throne that forgets its borrowed nature. The verse functions as Daniel's warning to Belshazzar that his father's history is about to repeat in his own house that very night, and as a standing warning to every reader that heart lifted up in pride is the precise hinge on which God removes rulers from thrones he alone establishes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DEPOSE: put down from a throne or high station; deprived of authority, rank, or office.
webster_full: DEPOSE, v.t. To put down from a throne or high station; to remove from office.
DEPOSED, pp. Put down; deprived of sovereignty or dignity.
In Daniel, used of Nebuchadnezzar's humbling after pride.
Spoken to Belshazzar as warning, hours before his own fall.
Treats the removal of a ruler as a direct act of divine judgment.
scriptures: But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him:
corruption_summary: Political analysis typically explains a ruler being deposed purely in terms of coups, economics, or military failure, leaving no room for Daniel 5:20's verdict that pride before God is the deeper and decisive cause.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel does not deny the visible mechanisms of Nebuchadnezzar's humbling; he simply insists they were not the ultimate cause. Heart lifted up, mind hardened in pride is named as the hinge, with the political and physical consequences following from it.

The corrective for a purely secular reading of history is not to deny secondary causes but to recover their subordination to this one: God deposes those he has himself raised, on his own timetable, for his own stated reason, regardless of how stable any throne appears from the inside.
roots_summary: Aramaic andachat, related to bringing down or causing to descend, the standard term in Daniel's Aramaic chapters for the removal of a ruler from power.
roots_lines: Deposed names the removal of a ruler, with divine judgment as its true cause.
Nebuchadnezzar's pride is named as the hinge of his fall.
Daniel delivers this history to Belshazzar as a direct warning.
Belshazzar's own fall follows that same night.
Every throne forgets its borrowed nature at its own peril.
usage: He was deposed from his kingly throne — pride's direct consequence.
They took his glory from him — total, not partial, humbling.
Spoken as warning to a king about to repeat the history himself.

pos: adj. (destructive to morals or society; noxious; mischievous in a dangerous degree)
etymology: Latin pestilens, from pestis, plague — originally of disease, extended to describe a person as a moral plague upon a community.
biblical_def:
For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.

Tertullus, the hired orator, levels this charge against Paul before Felix, and the word pestilent is chosen precisely for its force: it casts the gospel's spread, called here sedition, as a contagion to be contained rather than a message to be weighed. The accusation is false in substance — Paul has not stirred riots, he has preached Christ — but it is instructive in form, because it shows exactly how the world has always answered the gospel's advance: not usually by refuting it, but by rebranding its messengers as dangers to public order. Pestilent is the language of every age that would rather quarantine the truth than examine it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PESTILENCE: noxious to morals; mischievous to the public peace; dangerous in the manner of a plague.
webster_full: PESTILENCE, n. A contagious or epidemic disease; also, moral corruption.
PESTILENT, a. Producing pestilence; noxious to health; mischievous to morals or society.
Used figuratively, not literally, of a person or movement.
In Acts, a hired orator's accusation against Paul before Felix.
Shows how the gospel's advance was rebranded as a danger to public order.
scriptures: For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes:
corruption_summary: The impulse behind Tertullus's accusation persists wherever gospel conviction is recast, not as truth to be refuted, but as a social contagion to be managed, policed, or quarantined.
corruption_paragraphs: Pestilent fellow was never a serious engagement with Paul's teaching; it was a label designed to end the conversation by making the man himself the danger. The same move recurs whenever a culture prefers to diagnose believers as a public-health or public-order problem rather than answer their claims.

The corrective is Luke's own narrative structure: he records the false charge, then lets Paul answer it plainly and reasonably before Felix. The accusation of pestilence does not get the last word; the examined content of the faith does.
roots_summary: Greek loimos, pestilence, plague, used here as a term of abuse rather than literal disease — the same metaphor Webster's English preserves almost exactly.
roots_lines: Pestilent is a figurative accusation, not a literal diagnosis.
Tertullus uses it to recast gospel preaching as social contagion.
The charge against Paul is false in substance though vivid in form.
Labeling believers dangerous has always been easier than refuting them.
Luke lets Paul's reasoned answer, not the slur, have the final word.
usage: We have found this man a pestilent fellow — a hired accusation, not an argument.
A mover of sedition — gospel preaching recast as civil danger.
Paul answers the charge plainly rather than the charge silencing him.

pos: n. (seizure of property by lawful or state authority as a penalty)
etymology: Latin confiscare, from con- and fiscus, treasury — to transfer property into the state's treasury as punishment.
biblical_def:
And whosoever will not do the law of thy God, and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him, whether it be unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment.

This is Artaxerxes' decree empowering Ezra, and the striking feature is the yoking of the law of thy God with the law of the king under a single penalty scale. Confiscation of goods sits here as one tier among several — lighter than death or banishment, heavier than nothing — in a civil enforcement mechanism that a pagan emperor extends to Judah's returned exiles for the sake of good order in his empire. The verse is a reminder that God can use even a foreign king's penal code, confiscation included, as an instrument to protect the worship and conduct of his people in a specific historical moment, without that arrangement becoming a timeless pattern for church-state relations.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CONFISCATE: the act of seizing property for the public treasury, as a penalty for a crime or offense.
webster_full: CONFISCATE, v.t. To seize and adjudge to the public treasury, as a penalty.
CONFISCATION, n. The act of confiscating; forfeiture of goods to the state.
A tier of civil penalty, distinct from death, banishment, or imprisonment.
In Ezra, decreed by a pagan king to enforce obedience to God's law.
An instance of common grace used for a specific historical purpose.
scriptures: And whosoever will not do the law of thy God, and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him, whether it be unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment.
corruption_summary: Debates over church and state often read Ezra 7:26 as a model to replicate, missing that this is a specific Persian civil decree for a specific historical moment, not a timeless template for enforcing religion by confiscation or any other state penalty.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to treat Artaxerxes' decree as proof that God endorses state enforcement of religious law in every age. The text records what God providentially used in Ezra's specific circumstance; it does not thereby authorize confiscation of goods as a standing tool of church discipline or civil religion generally.

The sounder reading keeps the verse in its place: an instance of common grace, where a pagan ruler's self-interest in a well-ordered province happened to serve the restoration of right worship, without collapsing the distinction between civil penalty and the church's own, very different, tools of discipline.
roots_summary: Aramaic nekasin, goods or property, paired with a verb of seizure — the term is administrative rather than theological, drawn from Persian imperial legal vocabulary.
roots_lines: Confiscation names a tier of civil, not ecclesiastical, penalty.
Artaxerxes' decree yokes the law of God and the law of the king.
It applies to a specific historical moment in Ezra's restoration.
God can use a pagan ruler's penal code for his own purposes.
The decree is not a timeless template for church-state enforcement.
usage: To confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment — one tier in a civil penalty scale.
Decreed by Artaxerxes, a pagan king, for a specific historical purpose.
An instance of common grace serving the restoration of worship.

pos: n. (a spreading over or across the whole of a surface or situation)
etymology: OVER + SPREAD, Old English sprædan — to extend completely across or beyond the usual bounds.
biblical_def:
And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate, even until the consummation, and that determined shall be poured upon the desolate.

This clause sits at the center of Daniel's seventy weeks prophecy, among the most disputed and most structurally important verses in the Old Testament. Overspreading describes abominations not as an isolated act but as something that covers, saturates, the whole situation — total corruption of what should have been sacred space, provoking total desolation in response. Whatever the precise historical referent (interpreters have long debated Antiochus Epiphanes, the Roman desolation of the temple, and the final Antichrist as layered or successive fulfillments), the pattern itself is clear and repeated throughout Scripture: abomination that overspreads sacred space does not go unanswered, but is met with decreed, bounded desolation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from OVERSPREAD: spreading over the whole surface; covering completely, as a flood or a corrupting influence.
webster_full: OVERSPREAD, v.t. To spread over; to cover the whole surface of.
OVERSPREADING, n. or part. The act or state of spreading completely over.
Used of a totalizing corruption, not a partial or isolated act.
Central to Daniel's seventy weeks prophecy.
Pattern repeated throughout Scripture: total abomination met with decreed desolation.
scriptures: And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate, even until the consummation, and that determined shall be poured upon the desolate.
corruption_summary: Sensational prophecy teaching often treats overspreading of abominations as a cipher to be decoded for current-events speculation, losing the verse's own emphasis on a determined, bounded judgment rather than an open-ended puzzle.
corruption_paragraphs: Much popular prophecy writing mines this clause for headline-matching, rather than attending to what the text actually stresses: that determined shall be poured upon the desolate — judgment that is decreed, measured, and purposeful, not chaotic or indefinite.

The sounder reading holds the historical fulfillment (whether Antiochus, the Roman destruction of AD 70, or their typological pointing to a final Antichrist) humbly, while keeping firm what the text keeps firm: abomination that overspreads what is sacred will be met with desolation that is likewise total, and likewise determined by God, not by the one who causes it.
roots_summary: Hebrew kenaph shiqqutsim, literally wing of abominations, a vivid image of something spreading wide like a bird's wing, rendered overspreading to capture its totalizing reach.
roots_lines: Overspreading pictures abomination as a wing extended wide, not an isolated act.
The verse sits at the center of Daniel's seventy weeks prophecy.
Total corruption of sacred space provokes total, decreed desolation.
Interpreters debate the precise historical referent across the centuries.
The pattern of total abomination met with determined judgment is Scripture-wide.
usage: For the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate — total corruption, total consequence.
That determined shall be poured upon the desolate — judgment is decreed, not chaotic.
One of the most structurally important clauses in Daniel's prophecy.

pos: n. (an earnest request; urgent petitioning; entreaty)
etymology: Old French entraitier, from en- and traitier, to treat or negotiate — an earnest pleading that seeks to persuade.
biblical_def:
Praying us with much intreaty that we would receive the gift, and take upon us the fellowship of the ministering to the saints.

Paul describes the Macedonian churches, themselves in deep poverty, begging with much intreaty for the privilege of giving to the Jerusalem relief fund. The word reverses the direction readers expect: ordinarily the needy plead to receive, but here the giver pleads for the right to give. Intreaty names urgent, humble persistence applied not to a request for help but to a request to be allowed to help, and Paul holds this up as proof that true Christian generosity flows from grace received, not from surplus available — the Macedonians' deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality precisely because their giving was never contingent on comfort.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ENTREAT: earnest request; urgent solicitation; the act of pleading persistently for something desired.
webster_full: ENTREAT, v.t. To ask earnestly; to beseech; to petition with urgency.
INTREATY (ENTREATY), n. Earnest petition; urgent solicitation.
Here applied to a request to give, not a request to receive.
In 2 Corinthians, describes the Macedonian churches' giving.
Paired with deep poverty to show grace, not surplus, as the source of generosity.
scriptures: Praying us with much intreaty that we would receive the gift, and take upon us the fellowship of the ministering to the saints.
corruption_summary: Generosity is often marketed today as something that flows naturally from abundance, but 2 Corinthians 8:4 reverses that logic: the Macedonians' intreaty to give arose precisely out of their deep poverty, as evidence of grace rather than margin.
corruption_paragraphs: A prosperity-adjacent assumption treats giving as what the comfortable do once their own needs are met. Paul explicitly denies this sequence: the churches of Macedonia gave beyond their power, begging for the privilege, while in great trial of affliction and deep poverty.

The corrective recovers intreaty as evidence of grace already at work rather than a fundraising tactic to be replicated by pressure. Paul is careful, two verses later, to say he speaks not by commandment — the Macedonians' urgent request to give was theirs alone, unforced, and that is exactly what made it exemplary.
roots_summary: Greek parakalountes, from parakaleo, to call alongside, exhort, beseech — the same verb root rendered Comforter when applied to the Holy Spirit, here describing urgent human pleading.
roots_lines: Intreaty names urgent, humble, persistent pleading.
Here it is pleading to give, not pleading to receive.
The Macedonians' deep poverty is paired with abounding generosity.
True giving flows from grace received, not from available surplus.
Paul records the intreaty as voluntary, never commanded.
usage: Praying us with much intreaty — begging for the privilege of giving.
Deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality.
Generosity here is evidence of grace, not a product of margin.

pos: n. plural (the exercise of the prophetic gift; spoken declarations of God's revealed word)
etymology: Greek propheteia, via PROPHESY — the speaking forth of what God has revealed, whether foretelling or forth-telling.
biblical_def:
Despise not prophesyings.

This command sits among a rapid series of brief imperatives closing 1 Thessalonians — rejoice evermore, pray without ceasing, in every thing give thanks — and shares their urgency and brevity. Despise not prophesyings warns against a specific temptation in the early church: dismissing genuine spoken revelation, perhaps because it came through ordinary or unimpressive messengers, or because it was mixed in practice with counterfeits. Paul's very next command, prove all things, supplies the balance: the answer to possible abuse of prophesyings is not contempt but careful testing, holding fast what is good while rejecting what fails the test. The church is never told to silence the gift; it is told to stop despising it and start discerning it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PROPHESY: the act of uttering predictions or declarations under divine inspiration; the exercise of the prophetic office.
webster_full: PROPHESY, v.i. To foretell future events; to utter predictions under divine inspiration.
PROPHESYING, n. The act or practice of prophesying; a spoken declaration of revealed truth.
Here plural, describing the ongoing exercise of the gift in the assembly.
Commanded not to be despised, immediately followed by a command to test it.
Balances openness to genuine revelation with careful discernment.
corruption_summary: Churches tend to resolve the tension of this verse by collapsing it toward one extreme — either despising all claims to prophecy as inherently suspect, or accepting them uncritically — rather than holding Paul's own pairing of despise not with prove all things.
corruption_paragraphs: One error treats despise not prophesyings as a dead letter, assuming the gift ceased entirely and so the command no longer applies to anything. Whatever one's position on continuing gifts, the verse's logic — do not dismiss contemptuously what claims to be God's word without first testing it — remains a standing principle.

The opposite error treats any confident spoken claim as self-authenticating, skipping straight past prove all things to hold fast that which is good. Paul's two commands are a single unit: openness without discernment is as much a failure of this verse as contempt without a hearing.
roots_summary: Greek propheteias, plural of propheteia, prophecy — the standard New Testament term for the spiritual gift exercised in the assembly, distinct from the predictive sense alone.
roots_lines: Prophesyings names the exercise of the prophetic gift in the assembly.
Paul commands the church not to despise it.
The immediately following command is to prove all things.
Openness and discernment are paired, not opposed.
Neither blanket dismissal nor uncritical acceptance honors the verse.
usage: Despise not prophesyings — a warning against contemptuous dismissal.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good — the test that follows.
The gift is to be discerned, not silenced or swallowed whole.

pos: n. plural (severe whippings; sufferings inflicted by the lash)
etymology: Old French escorgier, to whip, from Latin excoriare, to flay — punishment inflicted by repeated lashing.
biblical_def:
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment.

This verse sits inside Hebrews 11's roll call of faith, but it marks a deliberate turn in the chapter: after a long list of those whose faith produced deliverance — the mouths of lions stopped, the violence of fire quenched — the writer turns to others whose faith produced only suffering, ending, several verses later, in death without rescue. Scourgings belongs to this second, harder category, and the chapter refuses to rank the two groups by outcome. Faith that endures mockings and scourgings without deliverance is named of equal standing with faith that escapes the lions' mouths; the world was not worthy of either, and both await the same better resurrection.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SCOURGE: severe whippings inflicted as punishment; sufferings endured by repeated lashing.
webster_full: SCOURGE, v.t. To whip severely; to lash; to punish with stripes.
SCOURGINGS, n. plural. Instances or sufferings of severe whipping.
Grouped with mockings, bonds, and imprisonment in Hebrews 11.
Marks the chapter's turn from deliverance-faith to endurance-faith.
Given equal standing with miraculous deliverance as true faith.
scriptures: And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:
corruption_summary: A faith culture oriented toward visible breakthrough and deliverance testimonies can quietly rank the lion's-mouth faith of Hebrews 11 above the scourgings faith of the very same chapter, exactly the ranking the text itself refuses to make.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation is to read Hebrews 11 as building toward ever more impressive victories, treating unrescued suffering as a lesser or incomplete faith. The chapter structure argues otherwise: it moves deliberately from deliverance to scourgings, torture, and death without a hint that the second group's faith was inferior.

The corrective is the chapter's own closing verdict: these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise, God having provided some better thing for us. Scourgings endured in faith are not faith's failure but its proof, awaiting a resurrection better than any rescue in this life.
roots_summary: Greek mastigon, from mastix, a whip or scourge — the same root used of the physical scourging of Christ himself before the crucifixion.
roots_lines: Scourgings names severe, repeated whipping endured for faith.
Hebrews 11 pairs it with mockings, bonds, and imprisonment.
The chapter turns here from deliverance-faith to endurance-faith.
Both kinds of faith receive the same verdict: well-attested, not inferior.
A better resurrection, not rescue in this life, is the promised reward.
usage: Cruel mockings and scourgings — faith that endures rather than escapes.
Grouped with bonds and imprisonment in the roll call of faith.
The world was not worthy of them — equal honor with the deliverance-faithful.

pos: n. plural (prideful, puffed-up conduct; arrogant disturbances within a community)
etymology: Old English swellan, to swell, grow distended — figuratively, pride or faction puffing a person or group beyond its proper measure.
biblical_def:
For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults.

Paul's list reads almost as a clinical description of a church eaten from within, and swellings sits near its climax, just before tumults. The image is deliberately physical: pride distends a person or a faction the way disease distends a body, an unnatural inflation that has nothing to do with healthy growth. Paul fears finding the Corinthians still disfigured this way on his next visit, and the verse that follows names the specific sin he expects to have to mourn — uncleanness unrepented of. Swellings is not a minor social friction in Paul's accounting; it belongs on the same list as wraths and strifes, a mark of a congregation still governed by flesh rather than by the Spirit he has spent two long letters trying to correct.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SWELL: a distended, puffed-up state; figuratively, pride, arrogance, or faction disturbing the peace of a community.
webster_full: SWELL, v.i. To grow larger; to be distended; figuratively, to become proud or arrogant.
SWELLINGS, n. plural. Instances of prideful or factious disturbance; tumid, puffed-up conduct.
Used figuratively of a community's internal disorder, not a physical ailment.
Listed by Paul among the sins he fears finding still present at Corinth.
Grouped with debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, and tumults.
scriptures: For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults:
corruption_summary: Modern church culture often treats factional pride and backbiting as mere personality conflict or organizational friction, while Paul lists swellings among sins requiring the same mourning and repentance as sexual uncleanness in the very next verse.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy to read debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults as unfortunate but low-grade social dysfunction, the kind every organization has. Paul's placement argues otherwise: this list sits in the same breath, the very next verse, as uncleanness and fornication unrepented of.

The corrective is to take swellings as seriously as the Corinthians were tempted to take it lightly — not a personality clash to be managed but a fleshly disorder to be mourned and repented of, because a congregation still governed by prideful faction has not yet been governed by the Spirit Paul labored to give it.
roots_summary: Greek physioseis, from physioo, to puff up, the same root Paul uses earlier in 1 Corinthians of knowledge that puffeth up — binding this swelling to pride of mind as much as pride of faction.
roots_lines: Swellings pictures pride as an unnatural, disease-like distension.
It sits near the climax of Paul's list of feared Corinthian sins.
The same root elsewhere describes knowledge that puffeth up.
Paul groups it with wraths and strifes, not with minor friction.
The very next verse pairs it with unrepented uncleanness.
usage: Debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults — a full catalogue of fleshly church disorder.
Paul fears finding these still present on his next visit.
Grouped as seriously as sins requiring mourning and repentance.
